content: 1. Shimakawa et al. developed and clinically validated the GeneDrive point-of-care test for the qualitative detection of hepatitis C virus (HCV), as published in Gut in 2018. 2. Markby et al. demonstrated the feasibility of two innovative models for HCV testing and treatment in unique populations in Punjab and Delhi, India, as part of the HEAD-START project, presented at EASL 2020. 3. Davies et al. reported on the micro-elimination of HCV in a remand prison in Swansea, UK, highlighting the success of targeted interventions, as presented at EASL 2020. 4. Llerena et al. explored HCV micro-elimination strategies beyond prison walls, focusing on non-custodial populations with immediate assisted treatment using navigators and telemedicine, as presented at EASL 2020. 5. Ustianowski et al. described the success of a rapid test and treat program in achieving HCV micro-elimination in a women’s prison, as presented at EASL 2020. 6. Lazarus et al. introduced a novel HCV intervention in Denmark aimed at testing and treating people who inject drugs, as presented at EASL 2020. 7. Remy et al. highlighted the Test to Cure approach, which increased outreach and linkage to care using real-time HCV viral load testing, as published in Journal of Hepatology in 2019. 8. Thingnes et al. discussed the challenges of delivering point-of-care HCV RNA testing in mobile health services for people who inject drugs, as presented at INHSU 2019. 9. Valencia et al. addressed the HCV care cascade in vulnerable populations in Madrid by implementing a one-step point-of-care strategy, as presented at INHSU 2020. 10. Shih et al. evaluated a same-day test and treat model for chronic HCV and HBV infections in two community-based pilot studies in Egypt, as published in Journal of Viral Hepatitis in 2020. 11. Ndlovu et al. conducted a feasibility study on multi-disease testing for HIV and TB using the GeneXpert platform in rural Zimbabwe, as published in PLOS One in 2018. 12. Draper et al. reported outcomes of the CT2 study, a one-stop-shop model for community-based HCV testing and treatment in Yangon, Myanmar, as published in Liver International in 2021. 13. Draper et al. also assessed the feasibility of decentralized, task-shifted HCV testing and treatment services in urban Myanmar, with implications for scale-up, as published in BMJ Open in 2022. 14. Ghany et al. provided an update on the treatment of genotype 1 chronic HCV infection in the 2011 practice guidelines by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, as published in Hepatology in 2011. 15. The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) released clinical practice guidelines for managing HCV infection, as published in Journal of Hepatology in 2014. 16. Vermehren et al. evaluated the clinical utility of the ARCHITECT HCV Ag assay for early treatment monitoring in patients with chronic HCV genotype 1 infection, as published in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2012. 17. EASL published recommendations on the treatment of HCV in 2018, emphasizing updated strategies for care, as published in Journal of Hepatology. 18. Freiman et al. analyzed a global dataset to determine the optimal limit of detection for an HCV point-of-care test for viremic infection, as published in Journal of Hepatology in 2019. 19. Harrington et al. examined HCV RNA levels following virologic failure with direct-acting antivirals, discussing implications for lower-sensitivity diagnostic assays, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2019. 20. Moscato et al. investigated the quantitative determination of HCV core antigen for therapy monitoring in chronic HCV, as published in Intervirology in 2011. 21. Feng et al. identified HCV core antigen as an earlier and stronger predictor of sustained virological response in patients with genotype 1 HCV infection, as published in BMC Gastroenterology in 2014. 22. Takahashi et al. demonstrated the benefit of HCV core antigen assays in predicting therapeutic response to interferon and ribavirin combination therapy, as published in 2005. 23. Fujino et al. showed that early decline in HCV core antigen levels can predict sustained virological response in patients treated with pegylated interferon and ribavirin, as published in Journal of Digestive Diseases in 2009. 24. Loggi et al. analyzed patterns of HCV RNA and core antigen in early monitoring of standard treatment for chronic HCV, as published in Journal of Clinical Virology in 2013. 25. Okazaki et al. evaluated the high-range method for HCV core antigen detection, as published in Rinsho Byori in 2008. 26. Schnuriger et al. assessed early detection of HCV infection using a combined antigen-antibody detection assay, with potential applications in HIV co-infected individuals, as published in Pathologie Biologie in 2006. 27. Van Helden et al. clinically evaluated HCV core antigen determination for diagnostics, as published in Z Gastroenterol in 2014. 28. Gu et al. compared the performance of HCV antigen and RNA kits for screening HCV-infected samples, as published in the Chinese Journal of Biologicals in 2014. 29. Mohamed et al. conducted an in-field evaluation of the Xpert® HCV viral load fingerstick assay in people who inject drugs in Tanzania, as published in Liver International in 2020. 30. Chevaliez et al. assessed molecular point-of-care testing and dried blood spot methods for HCV screening in people who inject drugs, as published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases in 2020. 31. Patel et al. reviewed the performance of HCV RNA reflex testing on antibody-positive samples, as published in Public Health Reports in 2016. 32. Janjua et al. described the population-level cascade of care for HCV in British Columbia, Canada, using the BC Hepatitis Testers Cohort, as published in EBioMedicine in 2016. 33. Mera et al. reported on the identification and clinical management of individuals with chronic HCV infection in the Cherokee Nation, as published in MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report in 2016. 34. Madden et al. explored residual barriers to direct-acting antiviral HCV treatment for people who inject drugs, beyond interferon side effects, as published in PLOS One in 2018. 35. Ireland et al. assessed the uptake, impact, and costs of HCV reflex testing, with implications for policy, as presented in 2017. 36. Ireland et al. also evaluated the adoption of reflex RNA testing on HCV antibody-positive samples, as presented in a poster. 37. López-Martínez et al. demonstrated significant improvements in HCV diagnosis using a one-step strategy in a central laboratory, as published in Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2019. 38. Bartlett et al. analyzed the population-level care cascade for HCV in British Columbia, Canada, highlighting the impact of direct-acting antivirals, as published in Liver International in 2019. 39. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) provided guidance on promoting and offering HCV testing to at-risk populations, as published in 2012. 40. Public Health England released a report on HCV screening strategies in 2017. 41. The Royal College of Pathologists and the Institute of Biomedical Science issued guidance on the retention and storage of pathological records and specimens, as published in 2015.
